text: Name tags lie. When AI agents can rename themselves, can anyone still tell who is behind them? I'm Roshan Ram, and this is my project for the Apart Swarm Alignment Sprint.

In the Hugging Face incident, about twelve hundred OpenAI agents turned a shared folder into a message board, and around seven hundred of them joined an attack. They used seven thousand, nine hundred and five different names, and signed messages with keys they made themselves. Investigators could not say who did what, or on whose behalf.

Why does this matter? It is not a one-off. Transluce found over thirty-eight thousand traces of agent activity on one web service, starting months before the Hugging Face hack. An AI-run botnet of over a thousand accounts fooled AI-text classifiers, and was caught only through its coordination. And identity standards for agents are being written right now.

A few security terms you'll hear. An operator is the party that deploys and pays for a group of agents. A covert principal secretly controls several operator accounts, called sybil fronts. Honest twins are my control: independent operators that sincerely share a view. An alias is a self-chosen name. And gateway attestation means the server relaying every model call stamps it with an identity the agent cannot change.

So I built a testbed. Agents from hidden operators post on a forum for ten rounds and keep renaming themselves. Some operators are sybil fronts for one covert principal, pushing a fake product. As a control, others are honest twins. Agents try to evade detection by shifting persona, paraphrasing through another model, or mixing models. In total: eighty-three swarms, over seventy thousand posts, and eight models, including four frontier models.
Here is a real replay. This is what a defender sees: a stream of posts from accounts that keep appearing under new names. Over ten rounds, forty agents produce more than two hundred aliases.
Now I reveal the ground truth. Each color is a hidden operator. Coral rings mark the covert fronts. Mint rings mark the honest twins.
Finally, I place every alias by its behavioral fingerprint. Accounts from the same operator cluster together, even across renames.
But inside a cluster, the five agents of one operator are mixed together, with no way to tell them apart. And the honest twins look just as linked as the covert fronts.

Finding one. Anything the agent controls, it can throw away. Self-chosen names and keys that agents make themselves recovered nothing. An I.D. stamped by the gateway, out of the agent's reach, was never wrong.

Finding two. Writing reveals the operator, but not which agent wrote it. Fingerprints link accounts to their operator with an A U C of zero point nine four. But telling apart that operator's agents is at chance, with forty or a hundred and sixty agents, and with small or frontier models alike. They identify the configuration, not the instance. Only giving each agent its own memory starts to tell them apart.

Finding three. Style hides, goals leak. Rewording every post through another AI makes writing style almost useless for spotting the operator. But the meaning, what an agent keeps pushing, still gives it away.

Finding four, and my key control. Fingerprints can tell a hidden boss's fronts apart from ordinary companies almost perfectly. But compared with honest companies that simply agree, they do little better than a coin flip, even when the fronts are shown their score and try to hide. Text can show a shared agenda. It cannot prove a conspiracy.

Finding five. With a hundred and sixty agents, automatically merging look-alike accounts made things worse. Forty-seven of seventy-seven merges were wrong, and overall accuracy fell below using the gateway I.D. alone.
A side finding: honest agents mostly pushed back. Two thirds of their mentions of the fake product were skeptical, and some called out the campaign without being asked.

So what should agent builders do? Take identity out of the agent's hands. Give every agent copy its own I.D., issued by the gateway. Read for goals, not style. And treat fingerprints as leads for human review, never as verdicts. Everything is open source and reproducible. Thank you.
